quote: Gilbert, Tafarodi, and Malone’s paper was entitled “You Can’t Not Believe Everything You Read.”
content: The Spinozan model did not hold up as a general account of comprehension. When statements contradict what readers already know, they are rejected fast and without cognitive effort, and load does not make them more believed (Richter, Schroeder & Wöhrmann 2009); the asymmetry Gilbert found appears only for statements the reader has no basis to evaluate. The asymmetry also depends on the framing of the false statement: when "false" is informative about the world, it is encoded as readily as "true" (Hasson, Simmons & Todorov 2005), and a large memory study found that the original results are better explained by how truth and falsity tags are stored than by any initial acceptance (Nadarevic & Erdfelder 2013). What survives is narrow: under load, novel, unverifiable statements labeled false are sometimes remembered as true. Descartes was not refuted; a special case was found in which Spinoza's model fits.

quote: These non-busy participants recommended 7.03 years versus 6.03 years for criminals whose reports falsely exacerbated or falsely excused.
content: This is the essay's own evidence that the effect is a load effect, and it should have been the headline. Undistracted readers of the same reports showed a difference of one year, which was not significant; the near-doubling occurred only in subjects hunting for fives in a number stream while reading. The lesson, then, is not that we believe everything we read but that comprehension under divided attention leaves the rejection step unfinished, which is a claim about attention rather than about belief. The practical advice, be careful with the supermarket newspaper, is better supported by a different literature: corrected misinformation continues to influence reasoning even when the correction is understood and accepted (Lewandowsky et al. 2012), and that effect does not require distraction. The essay reached a defensible conclusion through the wrong study.
